newsitem.title: SOMALIA: British aid worker kidnapped in Somalia.
newsitem.headline: British aid worker kidnapped in Somalia.

text.p: A British aid worker with the British-based Save the Children Fund has been kidnapped in Somalia near the Ethiopian border, Somali businessmen contacted by radio from the central town of Belet-Tuen said on Saturday.
But aid agency sources in the Kenyan capital Nairobi played down the incident, saying talks were being held with a local militia group "to sort out a few misunderstandings."

The businessmen said the unnamed British woman, visiting Somalia from neighbouring Kenya, was taken away in the border town of Feerfeer by unidentified gunmen on Friday night. Three of her Somali colleagues were also taken.
"She was taken away by unidentified gunmen yesterday (Friday) afternoon," Abukar Ali, a businessman told Reuters by high frequency radio from Belet-Tuen.
Another one added: "She was taken together with three of her Somali colleagues. We do not know who did it. It could be Somali gunmen or even the Ethiopian army, no-one knows."
Lawless Somalia has been without a central administration since 1991 after rebels ousted late dictator Mohamed Siad Barre.
Kidnappings especially involving foreigners are very common in Somalia, where weapons are readily available.
Aid agency sources in Nairobi said the Fund was holding negotiations with the militia holding the British woman.

"We are not calling it a kidnap. But at the same time they are not free to wander off. They are being held pending negotiations on working and operational procedures in that region," an aid source in Nairobi told Reuters.
Save the Children Fund officials could not be reached for comment.

Two weeks ago, an Australian pilot held in jail in Somalia for more than four months was freed and flown to Kenya after Kenyan President Daniel arap Moi intervened successfully with south Mogadishu faction leader Hussein Aideed.
Justin Fraser was handed over to his mother, who had stayed in Nairobi for months and campaigned for his release, which came as a complete surprise after numerous false alarms.
He had been held since May in the southwestern Somali town of Baidoa by the south Mogadishu-based faction led by Aideed, who succeeded his father Mohamed Farah Aideed at his death on August 1.
Fraser was arrested in the town of Baidoa where he landed after his plane developed engine problems.
His plane was loaded with qat, the leaves and bark of a bush which when chewed acts as a mild stimulant. It is flown to Somalia daily in a multi-million dollar business from Kenya and Ethiopia.
